newsitem.title: GREECE: ELEFSINA-SPATA ROAD READY IN TIME FOR AIRPORT-MIN.
newsitem.headline: ELEFSINA-SPATA ROAD READY IN TIME FOR AIRPORT-MIN.

text.p: Greece's Public Works Minister Costas Laliotis said the planned 422 billion drachma Elefsina-Spata ring-road will be ready in time to link Athens with its new Spata airport, expected to open in February 2001.

"There is no ground for concern about the delays realised in the commencement of the project," Laliotis told Reuters. "The Elefsina-Spata autoroute will be completed in time for a link-up with the Spata airport."
Construction will be carried out by Attiki Odos, a consortium of Greek contractors led by Aktor. Works were supposed to start some three years ago.
"The Greek state would face substantial penalty clauses raised from the Hochtief-led consortium which is building the Spata airport if the ringroad is not ready on time," Laliotis said.
The Elefsina-Spata ring-road is a large infrastructure project included in the EU's TransEuropean Networks.
It will run from the outskirts of the Spata airport through the northern part of Athens and will be linked with Greece's main autoroute at Elefsina, east of Athens.
The road will be operated by Attiki Odos and France's Transroute Internationale, which will hold a 7.0 percent stake.
"There is positive progress but negotiations with the European Investment Bank over financial guarantees are laborious and time-consuming," said Leonidas Bobolas, managing director of Aktor.
"I believe the financing deal will be concluded around September 1997," he said.
But there were more reasons for ensuring that the new Spata airport would not be deprived of its vital road link to Athens.

"The ring-road project will be constructed in separate parts. We will give priority on those sections linking Spata to Athens over those on the western side towards Elefsina," George Ganotis, public works general secretary said.
"The Spata-Pallini section which will provide access to the airport from a major Attica motorway has a projected completion time of 3.5 years," Bobolas said.
"Hence, I firmly believe that the February 2001 deadline will be met by Attiki Odos," he added.
No significant difficulties were seen coming from the fair amount of expropriation involved in the project.
"The area which the road will run through is scarcely populated and houses only temporary facilities of small factories," Bobolas said.
"There are strict regulations on residential housing since the 1950s, when the project was initially conceived."
The Elefsina-Spata autoroute will run for 52 kilometres with three lanes on each direction plus a couple of emergency lanes.
A separate 20-kilometre section will also be constructed on the western foot of the Hymetos mountain, giving access to and from Athens' eastern and southern suburbs.
The project's 422.3 billion drachma budget (in 1994 prices) will be met by a 215.4 billion loan facility from the European Investment Bank and the Greek State, 125.5 billion.
The balance will be met by own equity and commercial bank loans.
